prompt: You are designing the state layer for a multi-tenant insurance agent platform where one customer's case is worked by a triage agent, an underwriting agent, and a billing agent across many turns and sessions. You must retain (1) the current conversation's short-term working state, (2) facts shared across all agents on the same case (the team state), and (3) durable customer facts that must persist across cases and sessions. Tenant data must be isolated so Carrier A's memory can never be retrieved while serving Carrier B. Which state persistence design is correct?
options: Persist everything into one global semantic memory index shared by all tenants and rely on the model's prompting to avoid cross-tenant recall.
Store all three tiers in the agent's in-memory context and re-send the full history each turn so no external store is needed.

Keep short-term state in the session, keep the shared case state in a scoped team/thread store, and keep durable customer facts in a long-term semantic memory index that is partitioned by tenant and filtered by a mandatory tenant key on every retrieval.
Keep only long-term memory and let each agent reconstruct short-term and team state by re-querying the vector store on every turn.
explanation: Multi-tier state persistence separates session state, shared team state, and long-term semantic memory, each with a different lifecycle. A mandatory tenant-key filter on every retrieval is what actually enforces tenant isolation in a shared store; a global unfiltered index risks cross-tenant recall, in-memory storage overflows the context window, and reconstructing everything from a vector store each turn is slow and expensive.

prompt: An orchestrator in a long-running procurement workflow accumulates context across 40 turns. Around turn 25, the agent begins to contradict decisions it made early on and re-asks for facts the user already provided (an entity continuity problem). You need to keep the agent coherent without exceeding the context window. Which context-management approach should you implement?
options: Periodically compact the conversation by summarizing completed segments while preserving entities, decisions, and open actions, and inject only the compacted summary plus the recent turns.
Raise the model's max_tokens to the maximum so the full transcript always fits.
Drop all turns older than the last five and re-derive everything from scratch.
Disable compaction and always re-send the complete raw transcript to guarantee no information is lost.
explanation: Semantic compaction preserves entity continuity and prior decisions while staying within the context window. Raising max_tokens does not overcome a finite window over a long transcript, dropping old turns loses early constraints, and resending the raw transcript overflows the window and inflates cost.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: A six-agent system (an orchestrator plus five subagents) intermittently produces wrong final answers, but the logs show each subagent reported success. You need cross-agent trace correlation, a record of each agent's reasoning path, and the ability to replay a failed run for debugging. Which observability design satisfies all three requirements?
options: Log only each subagent's final answer with a timestamp, since intermediate reasoning is not needed.
Give each agent an independent random trace ID so failures are isolated.
Capture only the orchestrator's input and output and assume subagents behave correctly.

Propagate a single correlation ID from the orchestrator through every subagent call, emit structured spans for each reasoning step and tool call, and persist the full span tree so a run can be replayed.
explanation: Cross-service trace correlation, structured logging of agent reasoning paths, and agent replay capture are all called out in the exam skills. Propagating one correlation ID through the whole span tree is the mechanism that ties the subagent calls together and enables replay. Per-agent random IDs, final-answer-only logging, and orchestrator-only capture all lose the cross-agent causal chain needed to debug the failure.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: A user-facing agent must call a downstream HR API to fetch only the records the signed-in user is allowed to see. A security review forbids granting the agent a service identity with broad access and forbids impersonating the user with a stored credential. Which authentication flow should the agent use?
options: Use a client credentials grant with a single service principal that can read all HR records.
Use OAuth 2.0 On-Behalf-Of (OBO) flow: the agent exchanges the user's delegated token for a scoped token to call the downstream API, preserving least privilege and per-user attribution.
Embed the user's password in the agent configuration so it can authenticate as the user.
Use a shared API key stored in plain text in the agent's prompt.
explanation: On-Behalf-Of preserves the delegated scope of the signed-in user, so the agent can only see what that user can see, while keeping per-user attribution and least privilege. Client credentials grant broad service-level access, embedding a password violates the no-impersonation rule, and a shared plain-text key is insecure.

prompt: You are designing a Zero Trust multi-agent deployment with an orchestrator, a billing agent, and a document agent. The document agent needs read access to a storage account; the billing agent needs write access to a billing database. A security requirement states that if the document agent is compromised, the attacker must not be able to move laterally to billing. Which design best satisfies this requirement?
options: Grant all agents a single subscription-contributor identity so each call never fails.
Give each agent its own scoped managed identity with only the permissions it needs, place resources behind private network boundaries, and deny cross-resource access from other agent identities.
Give the orchestrator full access to every resource so it can act on behalf of any agent.
Use one shared API key with all permissions, rotated yearly.
explanation: Zero Trust multi-agent solutions require per-agent identity scoping, lateral movement prevention, and least privilege. Giving each agent a scoped identity with only its own permissions and isolating resources on private networks prevents a compromised document agent from reaching billing. A shared contributor identity, an all-powerful orchestrator, and a shared key all widen the blast radius and defeat the requirement.

prompt: A document-extraction subagent calls an OCR tool that intermittently returns HTTP 429 (rate limited) or malformed JSON. When this happens the agent currently crashes the whole workflow. You must add robust error handling and a fallback path without human intervention. Which approach is best?
options: Implement retry with exponential backoff for transient errors, validate tool results, and fall back to a secondary extraction tool when the primary fails, surfacing a structured error to the orchestrator when both fail.
Remove the tool and hard-code the extraction logic into the prompt.
Return an empty result and let the final answer agent guess the content.
Add a human approval step for every single tool call to prevent any error.
explanation: Tool error handling, fallback mechanisms, and tool result validation are explicit exam skills. Retrying transient failures with backoff, validating the JSON, and falling back to a secondary tool keeps the workflow resilient without a human in the loop. Hard-coding, returning empty results, and human-approving every call all degrade correctness or add needless latency.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: A research agent sometimes enters a loop, repeatedly calling the same search tool with nearly identical queries and consuming tokens until it hits the model's output limit. You must bound cost and latency while still allowing legitimate multi-step research. Which control set is most appropriate?
options: Remove iteration limits so the agent can always finish, and simply raise the model's max output tokens.
Restrict the agent to a single tool call per run so it can never loop.
Only monitor token usage after the fact and take no runtime action.
Set a maximum number of iterations and a per-run tool-call budget, detect duplicate or near-duplicate tool calls to break loops, and terminate with a partial answer when limits are hit.
explanation: Token-limit and loop-control optimization means imposing iteration caps and tool-call budgets, detecting duplicate calls, and terminating gracefully. Removing limits increases cost, a single tool call cripples legitimate multi-step research, and after-the-fact monitoring does not stop a runaway loop.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: Agents in production need credentials for three downstream services, TLS certificates for mutual TLS, and signing keys that must be rotated every 90 days. Secrets must be accessed with least privilege and never stored in agent code or prompts. Which design is correct?
options: Store secrets, certificates, and keys in Azure Key Vault, grant agents access via their managed identities using Key Vault RBAC data-plane roles scoped per secret, and rotate with versioned references.
Hard-code the credentials in environment variables baked into the agent image.
Put all secrets in a single .env file committed to source control for easy distribution.
Use one vault-wide shared access policy granting all agents full get and list on the entire vault.
explanation: The prescribed secrets-management pattern is Key Vault plus managed identity plus Key Vault RBAC data-plane roles scoped per secret, with rotation via versioned references. Baking secrets into images, committing them to source control, and vault-wide shared policies all violate least privilege and rotation requirements.

prompt: A workflow has three stages: (a) high-volume request triage needing fast, cheap classification; (b) complex legal reasoning over long documents needing strong reasoning and large context; and (c) occasional fine-grained code generation. You must minimize cost and latency while meeting each stage's quality bar. How should you match models to tasks?
options: Use the single largest, most expensive model for all three stages to guarantee quality.
Use the smallest model for all stages to minimize cost regardless of quality.
Let every stage call every available model and vote on the answer.
Route each stage to a model sized to its task: a small fast model for triage, a large-context reasoning model for legal analysis, and a code-specialized model only when needed.
explanation: The skill 'match task demands to model family capacities' means right-sizing each stage's model: cheap and fast for triage, strong reasoning and large context for legal work, and a specialized model only when code generation is actually needed. Using one oversized model everywhere wastes cost, an undersized model degrades quality, and model voting multiplies cost with no reliability gain.

prompt: A support agent consistently fails to classify requests into your 14 internal categories that use company-specific terminology. Prompting with examples helps only partially. You are considering fine-tuning. Which strategy is correct?
options: Fine-tune a large frontier model on the entire production log verbatim, including PII.
Fine-tune once and never again because fine-tuning is permanent.
Fine-tune a small base model on a representative labeled dataset covering all 14 categories, and re-fine-tune when data drifts measurably rather than on a fixed schedule.
Skip fine-tuning and rely on increasing the number of few-shot examples without bound.
explanation: A fine-tuning strategy should use a right-sized model and a representative labeled dataset that covers all categories, with PII scrubbed and refresh driven by measured drift, not a fixed calendar. Fine-tuning a frontier model on raw PII-laden logs is wasteful and non-compliant, treating fine-tuning as permanent ignores drift, and unbounded few-shot examples inflate cost without converging.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: You need a continuous-improvement loop that automatically finds quality regressions and feeds improvements back into prompts and evaluations. Which pipeline is most complete?
options: Manually review a random sample of outputs once a quarter with no automated metrics.

Generate a synthetic regression dataset, run LLM-as-a-judge evaluations against it and against golden examples, capture user feedback, and use a semantic optimization loop to propose prompt or agent changes that are gated by the evaluations.
Only measure latency and throughput and ignore output quality.
Deploy prompt changes directly to production whenever a developer feels the output improved.
explanation: Continuous improvement combines synthetic data generation, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, golden examples, user feedback loops, and a semantic optimization loop whose proposed changes are gated by evaluation before release. Quarterly manual review, latency-only metrics, and gut-feel deployments all fail to detect or prevent regressions.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: A customer-facing agent can read a knowledge base, call a refund tool, and produce free-form replies. A review demands guardrails that catch unsafe user inputs, block harmful tool calls, and filter the final response. Which guardrail strategy is correct?
options: Implement multi-intervention guardrails at four points: validate user input, gate tool calls, validate tool responses, and filter the final output, each with its own policy.
Apply a single input filter and assume the rest of the pipeline is safe.
Only filter the final output after everything has already executed.
Disable guardrails in production to reduce latency and rely on the model's built-in safety.
explanation: The multi-intervention guardrail strategy explicitly covers user inputs, tool calls, tool responses, and outputs. Input-only filtering leaves tool-call and response paths open, output-only filtering lets harmful tool calls execute first, and disabling guardrails in production removes the safety layer entirely.

prompt: A financial agent can draft trades, but compliance requires that (1) low-risk trades under $1,000 execute automatically, (2) trades over $1,000 require human approval, and (3) the user is always shown what the agent is about to do and why. Which design satisfies all three requirements?
options: Let the agent execute all trades automatically regardless of amount to maximize efficiency.
Require human approval for every single action including low-risk trades, removing all autonomy.
Hide the agent's reasoning to avoid overwhelming the user and execute silently.
Define autonomy levels with tiered human-in-the-loop gating by action risk, and provide transparency affordances that show planned actions and rationale before execution.
explanation: The design needs graded autonomy levels plus tiered human-in-the-loop gating tied to action risk, along with human-AI experience (HAX) transparency showing what will happen and why. Full autonomy, zero autonomy, and hidden reasoning each violate at least one requirement (safety, efficiency, or transparency).

prompt: An agent repeatedly sends a long static system prompt plus a large, mostly-unchanged knowledge payload on every turn, and users ask many near-duplicate questions. You want to cut cost and latency. Which caching strategy combination is most effective?
options: Disable all caching because caching can return stale answers.
Cache only the user's exact query string so nothing is ever reused across similar questions.
Use prompt caching for the stable system prompt and knowledge prefix, semantic caching for near-duplicate user queries, and response caching for exact-repeat questions.
Cache nothing but shorten the system prompt to a single word.
explanation: Prompt caching, semantic caching, and response caching solve different problems and should be used together: prompt caching reuses the stable prefix, semantic caching serves similar questions, and response caching serves exact repeats. Disabling caching, exact-string-only caching, and gutting the prompt all leave cost and latency on the table or harm quality.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: Six months after launch, a customer-service agent's answer quality silently degrades: it now refuses valid requests and adds fabricated policy details. You need to detect this drift early and trigger remediation automatically. Which monitoring design achieves this?
options: Rely on customer complaints to surface problems.
Monitor only the number of requests, since quality cannot be measured automatically.
Run a fixed golden-dataset evaluation on a schedule and on every deployment, compare evaluation metrics against a baseline, and raise alerts that trigger rollback or retraining when metrics regress.
Disable logging to protect privacy and skip evaluation.
explanation: Behavioral drift and quality regression detection require scheduled and per-deployment golden-dataset evaluations compared against a baseline, with alerting that triggers rollback or retraining. Complaint-driven or volume-only monitoring is reactive or blind to quality, and disabling logging removes the evidence needed to diagnose regressions.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: A regulated agent solution must prevent agents from calling arbitrary public endpoints and must keep data-plane traffic to a storage account and a search index on a private network. Which configuration is correct?
options: Leave the workspace on the public internet and rely on API keys for protection.
Enable the workspace managed virtual network with an allowlist and private endpoints so agents can reach only approved private endpoints and outbound internet is restricted.
Allow all egress so agents can reach any URL for maximum flexibility.
Disable network isolation but add a longer system prompt asking agents to be careful.
explanation: Network boundaries are a first-class security control: enabling the managed virtual network with private endpoints and an egress allowlist blocks arbitrary outbound calls and keeps data-plane traffic private. API keys alone do not create a network boundary, open egress defeats isolation, and prompt-based cautions are not a security control.

docs.label: Enterprise security in Azure AI Foundry

prompt: An orchestrator triggers long-running, stateful subagents that can take minutes and must survive transient failures, while the orchestrator itself is bursty and idle most of the time. You must meet reliability and cost requirements. Which compute design is best?
options: Run every agent on a single always-on VM sized for peak load.
Run all agents as one monolithic synchronous process with no queueing.
Run long-running subagents on durable, queue-triggered compute (such as Azure Container Apps jobs or Durable Functions) with checkpointing, and scale the lightweight orchestrator to zero when idle.
Use only scale-to-zero serverless for the long-running subagents and keep the orchestrator always on at peak capacity.
explanation: Long-running, stateful work belongs on durable, queue-triggered compute with checkpointing so it survives failures, while the bursty orchestrator should scale to zero to avoid idle cost. An always-on peak VM and a monolithic process both waste cost or fail under load, and scale-to-zero serverless is a poor fit for minutes-long stateful jobs.

prompt: Across 15 agents, every agent must log its inputs, authorize each tool call, and translate exceptions into a consistent format. Duplicating this logic per agent has caused drift. Which approach centralizes these concerns?
options: Copy-paste the same logging and authorization code into each agent so each is self-contained.
Skip logging and authorization in development and add them manually in production.
Require each agent to invent its own exception format for flexibility.
Implement shared middleware that intercepts every agent invocation to apply logging, authorization, and exception handling uniformly, so agents only implement business logic.
explanation: Reusable middleware for logging, authorization, and exception handling is an explicit exam skill. A single middleware layer applies these cross-cutting concerns uniformly and eliminates per-agent drift. Copy-paste, deferring to production, and per-agent formats all reintroduce inconsistency.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: A long document-analysis agent exhibits a specific failure: it correctly retrieves relevant passages from the vector store but cannot keep the thread of 'Customer X' consistent across many turns, occasionally attributing one customer's details to another. Which issue is this, and what fix is most appropriate?
options: Entity continuity failure — persist and re-inject a compact entity map (who is who and what belongs to whom) each turn so the agent keeps identity references consistent.
Sliding-window amnesia — increase the number of retained turns indefinitely.
Summary drift — stop summarizing entirely and keep raw text.
Vector-only recall — remove the vector store and rely on full-text search.
explanation: The symptom (retrieval works but identity references get crossed between turns) is entity continuity failure, and the fix is persisting and re-injecting a compact entity map. Indefinitely retaining turns, dropping summarization, and abandoning vector retrieval misdiagnose the problem and do not fix identity consistency.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: Two of your agents must be able to call each other's APIs and a shared data API in production, independent of any signed-in user. The security team requires short-lived tokens, no shared long-lived secrets, and revocation. Which authentication approach is correct?
options: Generate one long-lived shared API key and copy it into both agents' configuration.
Use OAuth 2.0 client credentials with per-agent managed identities or app registrations so each agent obtains short-lived scoped tokens for the services it is authorized to call.
Have both agents sign in as a single human user account and use that user's password.
Use no authentication between trusted internal services.
explanation: For service-to-service calls with no user, the client credentials flow with per-agent identities gives short-lived, scoped, revocable tokens and per-agent attribution. A shared long-lived key and a reused human password both violate the short-lived and no-shared-secret requirements, and no authentication defeats the security model entirely.

prompt: In a hub-and-spoke design, the hub must hand off compact context to a subagent and then receive only the subagent's result, while long-lived facts (such as the user's standing preferences) must be available to all agents. Which memory architecture is correct?
options: Keep long-lived facts in shared long-term memory that all agents read, and keep ephemeral per-task context in short-term (session) memory passed explicitly between the hub and the current subagent.
Pass the entire long-term memory into every subagent call and back every time.
Store all facts in short-term memory so they are lost when the session ends.
Keep long-term memory local to the hub and hide it from subagents.
explanation: Short-term (session) memory holds ephemeral per-task context handed off between the hub and the active subagent, while long-term memory stores durable facts all agents need. Passing all long-term memory on every call inflates tokens, storing everything short-term loses facts, and hiding long-term memory from subagents prevents them from using standing preferences.

prompt: An agent's system prompt contains a static company policy that changes quarterly, and per request it must inject only the customer data relevant to that request while resisting prompt-injection attempts embedded in uploaded documents. Which prompt strategy is correct?
options: Hard-code the policy into the model weights by re-deploying the model each quarter.
Inject the full customer database into every request so the agent never misses context.
Trust all uploaded document content and ignore injection risk.

Manage prompts under a versioned lifecycle with the policy injected dynamically at runtime from a source of truth, inject only per-request-relevant context, and add defensive guidelines that instruct the agent to treat document content as data, not instructions.
explanation: Prompt lifecycle management, dynamic context injection, and defensive guidelines are all explicit prompt-engineering skills. Versioned prompts pulled from a source of truth avoid redeploying the model, injecting only relevant context controls cost and distraction, and defensive guidelines mitigate prompt injection by treating retrieved content as data. Hard-coding, over-injecting, and trusting document content all fail.

domain: Evaluate, optimize, and monitor multi-agent solutions
prompt: Finance needs to attribute token and compute spend to each business unit and get alerted before monthly budgets are exceeded. Agents are tagged by team. Which cost-management design is correct?
options: Aggregate all spend into a single untagged pool and split it evenly each month.
Apply cost tags or labels to each agent's resources, set budgets with alerts per business unit, monitor token usage and quotas in Foundry and Azure Monitor, and report chargebacks by tag.
Ignore cost until the invoice arrives and then reconcile manually.
Disable quotas so teams are never blocked, and skip monitoring.
explanation: Cost management spans usage, quotas, allocations, and chargebacks. Tagging agent resources, setting per-unit budgets with alerts, monitoring token usage and quotas, and reporting chargebacks by tag enables attribution and early warning. Untagged pooling, invoice-time reconciliation, and disabling quotas all lose attribution or visibility.

domain: Secure, govern, and deploy multi-agent solutions
prompt: A multi-agent service must roll out a new agent version to production with the ability to instantly roll back if automated evaluations fail, and it must first pass through development, test, and acceptance stages. Which release methodology should you use?
options: Deploy straight from the developer's laptop to production and fix issues live.

Use a DTAP pipeline (development, test, acceptance, production) with blue/green deployment in production so the new version runs alongside the old and can be switched back instantly, plus canary rollout to a subset when needed.
Use a single shared environment for development, test, and production to save cost.
Roll out to 100% of users immediately with no rollback plan.
explanation: A DTAP pipeline promotes through staged environments, and blue/green (with optional canary) keeps the old and new versions side by side for instant rollback when automated evaluations fail. Laptop-to-production, a single shared environment, and a full rollout with no rollback all violate release-management and rollback requirements.

prompt: Users complain that a multi-agent assistant acts with no explanation, and regulators require that users can contest an automated decision and reach a human. Which set of controls should you design?
options: Execute silently for efficiency and require users to accept all outcomes.
Show a single final answer with no rationale and no recourse.

Provide transparency (show what the agent will do and why), afford control (approve, override, or cancel before high-impact actions), and offer an escalation path to a human for contestable decisions.
Allow the agent to override user objections when it is confident.
explanation: Human-AI experience (HAX) and responsible AI require transparency, user control, and human escalation. Silent execution, no-rationale answers, and letting the agent override objections all remove user agency and would fail the regulatory requirement to contest and escalate decisions.
